plain: A rope inside the knee running from the front of the tibia up and backwards to the femur. It stops the tibia sliding forwards and stops the knee twisting too far inwards.
detail: From the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia, passing upwards, backwards and laterally to the posteromedial surface of the lateral femoral condyle. Taut in extension. Poorly vascularised, so it heals badly.
clinical: Torn by a twisting injury on a planted foot — a very common sports injury. Tested with the anterior drawer and Lachman tests. Because its blood supply is poor, a complete tear usually needs reconstruction rather than repair.

plain: The stronger of the two cruciates. It stops the tibia sliding backwards under the femur, which matters most when you walk downhill or down stairs.
detail: From the posterior intercondylar area of the tibia, running upwards, forwards and medially to the anterolateral surface of the medial femoral condyle. Taut in flexion. The two cruciates cross like the limbs of an X — hence the name.
clinical: Torn by a blow to the front of a flexed knee — classically the 'dashboard injury' in a road accident. Tested with the posterior drawer test and by looking for a posterior sag sign.

plain: A broad flat band on the inner side of the knee that stops the knee bending sideways outwards.
detail: A flat band from the medial femoral epicondyle to the medial condyle and shaft of the tibia. Its deep fibres are firmly attached to the medial meniscus — unlike the lateral collateral ligament, which is separate from the lateral meniscus.
clinical: That attachment to the medial meniscus is why a blow to the outside of the knee can tear the ligament and the meniscus together. With the anterior cruciate, that makes the 'unhappy triad'. Tested by applying valgus stress at 30° of flexion.

plain: A rounded cord on the outer side of the knee, easily felt when you sit cross-legged. It resists the knee being pushed inwards.
detail: A cord-like band from the lateral femoral epicondyle to the head of the fibula. It stands free of the capsule and of the lateral meniscus, separated from them by the tendon of popliteus.
clinical: Because it is separate from the lateral meniscus, lateral-side injuries are less likely to involve the meniscus than on the medial side.

plain: A C-shaped pad of fibrocartilage that deepens the top of the tibia so the rounded femur sits in it properly, and cushions the load passing through the knee.
detail: Semicircular and wider behind than in front. Attached to the intercondylar area by its horns, to the capsule at its periphery, and firmly to the deep fibres of the medial collateral ligament.
clinical: Injured far more often than the lateral meniscus, precisely because it is tethered to the medial collateral ligament and so cannot move out of the way. Only the outer third has a blood supply, so peripheral tears can be repaired while central tears usually cannot.

plain: An almost circular cartilage pad on the outer half of the top of the tibia. It is more mobile than the medial one, which protects it from injury.
detail: Nearly a complete ring, with its horns attached close together in the intercondylar area. Separated from the fibular collateral ligament by the popliteus tendon, and connected to the femur by the meniscofemoral ligaments.
clinical: Its greater mobility means it is torn much less often than the medial meniscus.

plain: The pointed ends of each meniscus, anchoring it to the top of the tibia. They are tough attachments rather than cushioning cartilage, which is why they are grouped with the ligaments.
detail: Each meniscus is fixed by an anterior and a posterior horn inserting into the intercondylar area of the tibia. The horns of the lateral meniscus attach close together, which is what allows it to be so much more mobile than the medial.
clinical: A root tear — a tear of a horn at its tibial attachment — leaves the meniscus unable to resist being squeezed outwards under load. Functionally that is as bad as removing the meniscus, and it accelerates osteoarthritis.

plain: A small band running from the back of the lateral meniscus up to the femur, behind the posterior cruciate ligament.
detail: Passes from the posterior horn of the lateral meniscus to the medial femoral condyle, behind the posterior cruciate ligament. Helps pull the lateral meniscus forwards as the knee extends.

plain: A short band joining the front horns of the two menisci to each other.
detail: Connects the anterior horn of the lateral meniscus to the anterior horn of the medial meniscus, so they move together during flexion and extension.

plain: A broad band reinforcing the back of the knee capsule, formed from an offshoot of the semimembranosus tendon.
detail: An expansion of the semimembranosus tendon running upwards and laterally across the back of the capsule. It forms the floor of the popliteal fossa, and the popliteal artery lies directly on it.
clinical: Because the popliteal artery is pinned against this ligament, a posterior dislocation of the knee frequently injures the artery. Always check distal pulses after a knee dislocation.

plain: The kneecap — the largest sesamoid bone in the body, sitting inside the quadriceps tendon. It holds the tendon away from the joint, which makes the quadriceps pull much more efficiently.
detail: A triangular sesamoid bone within the quadriceps femoris tendon. Its posterior surface is covered with the body's thickest articular cartilage and articulates with the patellar surface of the femur.
clinical: It increases the leverage of the quadriceps by about 30%. It usually dislocates laterally; the horizontal fibres of vastus medialis obliquus and the prominent lateral femoral condyle are what normally prevent this.

meshNames: Quadriceps common tendon and patellar ligament.r
ta2: Tendo musculi quadricipitis femoris; Ligamentum patellae
plain: The quadriceps tendon comes down into the top of the kneecap; the patellar ligament carries the pull on from the bottom of the kneecap to the tibia. Together they straighten the knee.
detail: The four heads of quadriceps femoris unite into a common tendon inserting on the base of the patella. Below the patella the fibres continue as the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity. It is called a ligament, not a tendon, because it runs bone to bone.
clinical: This is the tendon struck to elicit the knee jerk (L3, L4). Traction at the tibial tuberosity in an adolescent causes Osgood–Schlatter disease.

plain: Fibrous straps on the inner side of the kneecap that stop it sliding outwards.
detail: Expansions from vastus medialis and the fascia lata passing to the patella and tibia, blending with the capsule.
clinical: Torn when the patella dislocates laterally, which is the usual direction of dislocation.

plain: A small triangular muscle at the back of the knee. It 'unlocks' the fully straightened knee so you can bend it again.
detail: From the lateral femoral condyle, inside the capsule, running downwards and medially to the posterior surface of the tibia above the soleal line. Supplied by the tibial nerve.
clinical: In full extension the knee is locked by medial rotation of the femur on the tibia. Popliteus laterally rotates the femur on the fixed tibia to unlock it — flexion cannot begin until it does.

plain: The teardrop-shaped part of the quadriceps just above and inside the knee. Its lowest fibres run almost sideways and pull the kneecap inwards.
detail: From the intertrochanteric line and medial lip of the linea aspera to the medial border of the patella and the quadriceps tendon. Supplied by the femoral nerve.
clinical: Its oblique lower fibres are the main check on lateral patellar dislocation, and they waste quickly after knee injury or surgery — which is why rehabilitation targets them so heavily.

plain: The place on the inner side of the top of the tibia where three tendons fan out together like a goose's foot.
detail: The conjoined insertion of sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus on the upper medial surface of the tibia. Remember the order front to back as 'Say Grace before Tea'.
clinical: The overlying bursa is a common cause of medial knee pain, especially in runners and in older patients with osteoarthritis.

plain: A cushion of fat sitting behind the patellar ligament, filling the space at the front of the joint.
detail: Lies between the patellar ligament and the synovial membrane, deep to the ligament and in front of the femoral condyles.
clinical: Richly innervated, so it is a genuine source of anterior knee pain when it becomes impinged or inflamed (Hoffa's syndrome).

plain: A small fluid-filled sac between the skin and the front of the kneecap, letting the skin glide over the bone.
detail: Lies between the skin and the lower half of the patella and the upper part of the patellar ligament. It does not communicate with the joint cavity.
clinical: Inflamed by prolonged kneeling — 'housemaid's knee'. Contrast with 'clergyman's knee', which is the subcutaneous infrapatellar bursa, lower down over the tibial tuberosity.

plain: A sac between the patellar ligament and the front of the tibia, cushioning the ligament as the knee bends.
detail: Lies between the lower part of the patellar ligament and the tibia, separated from the joint cavity by the infrapatellar fat pad.

plain: The main artery behind the knee. It is the deepest structure in the popliteal fossa, lying right against the bone and capsule.
detail: The continuation of the femoral artery beyond the adductor hiatus, ending at the lower border of popliteus by dividing into anterior and posterior tibial arteries. Gives the genicular branches that form the anastomosis around the knee.
clinical: Its deep position against the joint makes it very vulnerable in posterior knee dislocation and in supracondylar femoral fracture. Its pulse is hardest to feel of all the lower limb pulses — press deeply with the knee flexed and relaxed.

plain: A network of small arteries encircling the knee. It keeps blood flowing to the leg when the main artery is squeezed shut in full flexion.
detail: Formed by the superior and inferior medial and lateral genicular arteries with the descending genicular and descending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral. The middle genicular artery pierces the capsule to supply the cruciate ligaments.
clinical: This collateral circulation can maintain the limb if the popliteal artery is gradually occluded — but it is far too small to compensate for sudden occlusion after trauma.

plain: A nerve that winds round the outside of the top of the fibula, where it lies just under the skin against bare bone. That is what makes it the most commonly injured nerve in the leg.
detail: The smaller terminal branch of the sciatic nerve (L4–S2). Runs along the medial border of biceps femoris, crosses the lateral head of gastrocnemius, then winds round the neck of the fibula to divide into superficial and deep fibular nerves.
clinical: Damaged by a fibular neck fracture, a tight plaster cast, or prolonged crossed legs. The result is foot drop — loss of dorsiflexion and eversion — with a high-stepping gait and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot.

plain: The larger branch of the sciatic nerve. It runs straight down through the middle of the popliteal fossa and supplies the calf and the sole of the foot.
detail: L4–S3. The most superficial of the three main structures in the popliteal fossa — nerve, then vein, then artery from superficial to deep. Supplies the posterior compartment of the leg and, via the plantar nerves, the sole.
clinical: Remember the order in the popliteal fossa as NVA from the surface inwards. Injury causes loss of plantarflexion and inversion, and sensory loss over the sole — which risks unnoticed pressure ulceration.

plain: The longest vein in the body, running up the inner side of the leg. At the knee it passes a hand's breadth behind the medial border of the patella.
detail: Begins at the medial end of the dorsal venous arch of the foot, passes in front of the medial malleolus, up the medial side of the leg and thigh, and drains into the femoral vein at the saphenous opening. Accompanied by the saphenous nerve below the knee.
clinical: Its constant position in front of the medial malleolus makes it the site for an emergency venous cutdown. It is also the vein most often harvested for coronary artery bypass grafting, and the one that becomes varicose.

plain: The gap in the adductor magnus muscle through which the femoral vessels pass from the front of the thigh to the back of the knee.
detail: An opening between the adductor and hamstring parts of adductor magnus, at the junction of the middle and lower thirds of the thigh. The femoral artery and vein pass through it and are renamed the popliteal artery and vein.
clinical: This is the landmark that defines where the femoral artery becomes the popliteal artery.
